title: Optimising areas and lengths under constraints
transcript: An optimisation problem asks for the greatest or least possible result under a rule. First use the rule to express the possibilities in terms of one choice. Many rectangle problems reward balance. Show why the nearby legal sizes give the best area.

AMC practice may ask for the largest area or smallest required boundary. Write which quantity stays fixed. A Rossmoyne style question may require whole-number dimensions or one side against a wall. Give a reason that every other choice is worse.
A rectangle has perimeter thirty metres and width five metres. What is its area? Use half of the perimeter to find one width plus one length.
The perimeter has two copies of each side. Half is fifteen, so the length is fifteen minus five, which is ten. Multiply width by length. The area is fifty square metres.
A rectangle with whole-number side lengths has perimeter thirty. What is the greatest possible area? Compare side lengths close to each other with ones far apart.

If the longer side exceeds the shorter by at least two, moving one unit from the longer to the shorter makes their product larger. The sum of the sides stays fixed. The closest pair has lengths seven and eight. The greatest area is fifty-six square units.

Build a rectangular pen against a wall using exactly fifty-four metres of fencing. Fence only the other three sides, and use whole-number lengths. Find the largest area and the dimensions that give it.

If x is a side going out from the wall, there are two such sides. The remaining fenced side measures fifty-four minus twice x. Area is half the product of twice x and the remaining length. Those two factors have a fixed sum, so the best factors are as close together as possible. Twice x must be even. Check the even values closest to half of fifty-four.

The best widths are thirteen and fourteen metres. Both give an area of three hundred and sixty-four square metres. Any other candidate makes the two factors farther apart. The larger gap reduces their product, so no farther candidate can beat this result.

A side against a wall does not use fencing. Count only the two widths and the fenced length before writing the equation. The best real-number answer can break an integer rule. Compare the nearby whole-number possibilities around that balance point.

Write the fixed sum, boundary or budget. Reduce the possible outcomes to one variable. Show that moving towards balance increases the product until you reach the closest legal dimensions. Check any ties.
